Part I - Exploration of the Carrier On-Time Performance Dataset from Bureau of Transportation¶

by Soizic Bourgeois¶

Introduction¶

This document explores a dataset from Bureau of Transportation containing 2,000,000 flights in the United States, including carriers, arrival and departure delays, and reasons for delays from 1987 to 2020.

# extract files from archive and load csv
with tarfile.open("./data/airline_2m.tar.gz", "r:gz") as t:
    for filename in t.getnames():
        try:
            f = t.extractfile(filename)
            print(f'Extracted {filename}')
        except :
            print( 'ERROR: Did not find %s in tar archive' % filename)
        if filename[-4:]=='.csv':
            try:
                flights_df = pd.read_csv(f, low_memory=False, encoding='latin1')
                print(f"Successfully loaded {filename} with shape: {flights_df.shape}")
            except Exception as e:
                print(f"Error reading CSV: {type(e).__name__} - {e}")
            flights_df.head()
        else:
            print(f'File extracted is not a csv: {filename}')

We have a lot of them!

The columns starting with div are related to diverted flights, so it makes sense to miss values there. Same for the cancellation reason.

The columns stating the time each delay cause triggered also have a lot of null, which makes sense if the flights are on time.

What is the structure of your dataset?¶

The data consists of 109 features on 2,000,000 flights. Most of the data are numeric.

What is/are the main feature(s) of interest in your dataset?¶

There is a lot of features in this dataset. The main interest of the dataset is to analyse the delays that can happen when flying.

Given the information available to us, we can investigate where and in which circunstances these delays are most likely to happen.

Thus the ArrDelay and DepDelay are the main features we are interested in.

What features in the dataset do you think will help support your investigation into your feature(s) of interest?¶

DOT_ID_Reporting_Airline, ArrDelay, CRSElapsedTime, ActualElapsedTime, AirTime, Distance, CarrierDelay, WeatherDelay, NASDelay, SecurityDelay, LateAircraftDelay might be the most interesting features for our analysis.

These will let us provide a complete operational view of what drives flight delays and how severely they impact performance.

Functions used in the exploration¶

# function to add title and axes labels
def generate_title_and_axes(title, x_axis, y_axis):
    plt.title(title)
    plt.xlabel(x_axis)
    plt.ylabel(y_axis)
In [11]:
# function to generate a countplot with tilted axis labels
def countplot(df,x):
    sns.countplot(data=df, x=x)
    plt.xticks(rotation=45);
In [12]:
# function to generate a histogram with log-normal fit
def lognorm_comparison(col, xmin, xmax, tick_step, ymax=None):
    data = flights_df_clean[col].dropna()
    min_val = data.min()

    s, loc, scale = lognorm.fit(data, floc=min_val-1)

    x = np.linspace(xmin, xmax, 500)
    p = lognorm.pdf(x, s, loc, scale)

    sns.histplot(data, stat="density", kde=True)
    plt.plot(x, p, 'r--', linewidth=2, label=f'Log-Normal Fit')
    
    plt.xlim(xmin, xmax);
    if ymax:
        plt.ylim(0,ymax);
    plt.xticks(range(xmin, xmax+1, tick_step));
    plt.legend();
#     plt.show()
    
    return s, loc, scale
In [13]:
# function to generate the Q-Q graph of a log-normal fit
def lognorm_qq_graph(col, s, loc, scale):
    n_points = flights_df_clean.shape[0]
    qs = (np.arange(n_points) - .5) / n_points
    expected_vals = lognorm.ppf(qs, s, loc, scale)

    plt.scatter(expected_vals, flights_df_clean[col].sort_values())
    plt.plot([-500,500],[-500,500],'--', color = 'black')
    plt.axis('equal')
    generate_title_and_axes(f'{col} Q-Q graph for log-normal fitting', 'Expected Values', 'Observed Values')
In [14]:
# function to calculate R2 for a linear regression
def calculate_r2(model, x, y):
    predict = np.poly1d(model)
    return r2_score(y, predict(x))
In [15]:
# function to convert categories into intervals
def calculate_interval_ticks_labels(min, max, step):
    boundaries = np.arange(min, max, step)
    tick_labels = [f"<{boundaries[0]}"]
    for start, end in zip(boundaries[:-1], boundaries[1:]):
        tick_labels.append(f"[{start}, {end}[")
    tick_labels.append(f">{boundaries[-1]}")
    return tick_labels

What about the delay causes that are mentionned in the features? How do they rank to each other?

In [28]:
# Calculate total sum of delay for each root cause
delay_cols = ['CarrierDelay', 'WeatherDelay', 'NASDelay', 'SecurityDelay', 'LateAircraftDelay']

total_minutes = flights_df[delay_cols].sum().reset_index()
total_minutes.columns = ['DelayType', 'TotalMinutes']
total_minutes = total_minutes.sort_values(by='TotalMinutes', ascending=False)

# plot
sns.barplot(
            data=total_minutes, 
            x='DelayType', 
            y='TotalMinutes'
            )

generate_title_and_axes(
                        "Accumulated Delay Duration by Root Cause", 
                        "Delay Root Cause", 
                        "Total Delay Time (Minutes)"
                        )

plt.xticks(fontsize=8)
plt.show()

A late aircraft causes the more delays in terms of time. However a late aircraft means there has been a consequence of at least one of the other causes at the origin. So we could consider Carrier delays, which comes second, as the main reason for delays.

Discuss the distribution(s) of your variable(s) of interest. Were there any unusual points? Did you need to perform any transformations?¶

In [29]:
sns.histplot(flights_df_clean['ArrDelay'], kde=True);
plt.xlim(-60, 180);
plt.xticks(range(-60, 181, 20));
generate_title_and_axes('Arrival delay distribution', 'Arrival delay', 'Flights count')

The delay at arrival looks like a log-normal distribution with its long right tail.

In [30]:
s, loc, scale = lognorm_comparison('ArrDelay', -60, 180, 20)
generate_title_and_axes('Arrival delay distribution with Log-Normal fit', 'Arrival delay', 'Density')
In [31]:
# print Q-Q plot to confirm the log-normal fit
lognorm_qq_graph('ArrDelay', s, loc, scale)

Looking at the Q-Q plot, the data severely departs from the diagonal reference line: flight arrival delays do not follow a theoretical log-normal distribution.

Flight delays will be better described as a heavy-tailed empirical distribution rather than a simple log-normal curve.

What about departure delays?

In [32]:

generate_title_and_axes('Departure delay distribution with Log-Normal fit', 'Departure delay', 'Density')
In [33]:
lognorm_qq_graph('DepDelay', s, loc, scale)

Once again the Q-Q plot shows a large discrepency between the data and the reference line. Flight departure delays do not follow a theoretical log-normal distribution.

Flight delays will also be better described as a heavy-tailed empirical distribution rather than a simple log-normal curve.

Of the features you investigated, were there any unusual distributions? Did you perform any operations on the data to tidy, adjust, or change the form of the data? If so, why did you do this?¶

We filtered the data to keep only the last 20 years of data to ease the load on the compute that was not able to process such an amount of data for some graphs. The analysis will then focus on the most recent years, which would be the most important data in case we would like to predict any future delays.

Bivariate Exploration¶

Is there a clear relationship between late departure and late arrival?

In [34]:
sns.scatterplot(data=flights_df_clean, x='DepDelay', y='ArrDelay');
# Add trend
model = np.polyfit(flights_df_clean['DepDelay'].astype(np.float32), flights_df_clean['ArrDelay'].astype(np.float32), 1)
plt.plot(flights_df_clean['DepDelay'].astype(np.float32), model[0] * flights_df_clean['DepDelay'].astype(np.float32) + model[1], color="red")
generate_title_and_axes('Arrival delay vs Departure delay', 'Departure delay', 'Arrival delay')
In [35]:
calculate_r2(model, flights_df_clean['DepDelay'], flights_df_clean['ArrDelay'])
Out[35]:
0.8729530857177679

$R^{2}$ tells us that 87.3% of the variance in the arrival delay is explained by the model. Which means the linear model represneted by y = model[0] x + model[1] is a good representation of the relationship between departure delay and arrival delay

In [36]:
print(f'The model has the following equation: y = {model[0]}x + {model[1]}')

The model has the following equation: y = 1.0085281144590827x + -3.2361786504421612

Considering the existence of this model, we will focus on one of the variable of interests: ArrDelay

Is there a relationship between the Airline we are flying and the delay at arrival? Let's see for each airline the proportion of flights in each delay group using a stacked bar chart.

In [37]:
# prepare variables neeeded for the loop on the delay groups
airlines = flights_df_clean['Reporting_Airline'].unique()
airlines_counts = flights_df_clean['Reporting_Airline'].value_counts()
arrdelaysgrp_ordered = sorted(flights_df_clean['ArrivalDelayGroups'].unique())

baselines = np.zeros(len(airlines))
artists = []

for i in range(len(arrdelaysgrp_ordered)):
    # calculate the proportion of the category
    arrdelaygrp = arrdelaysgrp_ordered[i]
    inner_counts = flights_df_clean[flights_df_clean['ArrivalDelayGroups'] == arrdelaygrp]['Reporting_Airline'].value_counts()
    inner_props = inner_counts / airlines_counts
    # create the associated bars
    bars = plt.bar(
                    x = np.arange(len(airlines)),
                    height = inner_props[airlines],
                    bottom = baselines
                    )
    artists.append(bars)
    baselines += inner_props[airlines]
    
plt.xticks(np.arange(len(airlines)), airlines, rotation = 90)

# create the legend with the intervals instead of the category labels
interval_labels = calculate_interval_ticks_labels(-15, 195, 15)
legend_labels = [interval_labels[int(i) + 2] if -2 <= i <= 12 else str(i) for i in arrdelaysgrp_ordered]
plt.legend(reversed(artists), reversed(legend_labels), title= 'Arrival Delay Intervals (min)', framealpha = 1, bbox_to_anchor = (1, 0.5), loc = 6);

generate_title_and_axes(
                        "Proportion of Delay Intervals Across Reporting Airlines", 
                        "Reporting Airline", 
                        "Proportion of Flights"
                        )

We can see that 2 airlines (HA - Hawaiian Airlines and KH - Aloha Air Cargo) stand out by being mostly in advance or on time compared to the other airlines.

Talk about some of the relationships you observed in this part of the investigation. How did the feature(s) of interest vary with other features in the dataset?¶

  • We notcied that the departure delay and arrival delay have a linear model linking them together, so we excluded the departure delay from the investigation.
  • We also showed that 2 airlines stand out by being more on time/in advance than others.
  • Finally, we discovered that the most in advance flights tend to be flying on a slighly longer distance.

Did you observe any interesting relationships between the other features (not the main feature(s) of interest)?¶

We did observe the relationship between ArrivalDelayGroup and the Distance but ArrivalDelayGroup is based on the value of our main feature of interest.

Multivariate Exploration¶

We earlier noticed that the Late Aircraft and Carrier delay seem to be the root causes that trigger the most accumulated delays. We also saw that some airlines are more on time than others and that the on time flights seem to be a bit longer.

Let's explore a bit deeper the different root causes to see the impact of each of them by airline and distance.

In [39]:
# filter to keep only the flights which arrived late
flights_delayed_df = flights_df_clean[flights_df_clean['ArrDelay'] > 0].copy()

# let's add a column for delay type
delay_causes = ['CarrierDelay', 'WeatherDelay', 'NASDelay', 'LateAircraftDelay', 'SecurityDelay']
melted_flights_delayed_df = flights_delayed_df.melt(
                                                    id_vars=['ArrDelay', 'Reporting_Airline', 'Distance'], 
                                                    value_vars=delay_causes, 
                                                    var_name='DelayType', 
                                                    value_name='DelayMinutes'
                                                    )

g = sns.FacetGrid(melted_flights_delayed_df, col='DelayType', col_wrap=3, height=4, aspect=1.2, sharex=False, sharey=True)

g.map_dataframe(sns.scatterplot, x='DelayMinutes', y='ArrDelay', hue='Reporting_Airline', size='Distance', sizes=(20, 200), alpha=0.6)

g.set_axis_labels("Cause Delay Duration (Minutes)", "Total Arrival Delay (Minutes)")
g.set_titles(col_template="{col_name}")
g.add_legend(title="Airline / Distance (miles)")
plt.subplots_adjust(top=0.9)
g.fig.suptitle("Impact of Individual Delay Causes on Overall Arrival Delay", fontsize=20)

plt.show()

Looking at the graphs we can notice:

  • a diagonal x=y in most graphs that corresponds to the flights whose delay was entirely explained by the primary cause of the graph.
  • In the case of the security delays, a lot of the points are below the diagonal, meaning the delay got recovered.
  • a vertical line at 0 in all graphs that corresponds to the flights whose delay was entirely explained by the causes other than the primary one of the graph.
  • points in between these 2 lines where multiple factor contributed to the delay.
  • Security delay is the reason occuring less often.
  • The reporting airline is difficult to analyse on this graph as there is so many of them that the colors get mixed up
  • We can see points of different sizes all over each graph, which means long distance flights do not seem to be more delayed than others.

The scatter graphs do not enable us to properly see the frequency of delays for each root cause, let's investigate it.

In [40]:
# let's add a column for delay type
delay_cols = ['CarrierDelay', 'WeatherDelay', 'NASDelay', 'SecurityDelay', 'LateAircraftDelay']
df_delays = flights_df[['ArrivalDelayGroups'] + delay_cols].melt(
                                                                id_vars=['ArrivalDelayGroups'],
                                                                value_vars=delay_cols,
                                                                var_name='DelayType',
                                                                value_name='DelayMinutes'
                                                                )

# we keep only the flights that are late
df_delays = df_delays[df_delays['DelayMinutes'] >= 15].copy()

# calculate the delay intervals
interval_labels = calculate_interval_ticks_labels(-30, (df_delays['ArrivalDelayGroups'].max()+1)*15, 15)
df_delays['DelayInterval'] = df_delays['ArrivalDelayGroups'].apply(lambda g: interval_labels[int(g) + 2] if -2 <= g <= 12 else str(g))

# define the order we will plot each category and interval
delay_order = df_delays['DelayType'].value_counts().index
unique_groups = sorted(df_delays['ArrivalDelayGroups'].unique())
interval_order = [interval_labels[int(i) + 2] for i in unique_groups if -2 <= i <= 12]

# plot
g = sns.FacetGrid(
                data=df_delays, 
                col='DelayInterval', 
                col_order=interval_order,
                col_wrap=3, 
                height=3.5, 
                aspect=1.3, 
                sharex=False
                )

g.map_dataframe(sns.countplot, x='DelayType', order=delay_order, color='tab:blue')

g.set_xticklabels(labels=delay_order, rotation=45, ha='right', fontsize=9)
g.set_titles(col_template="Delay {col_name}")
g.set_axis_labels("Delay Root Cause", "Number of Delays")

plt.subplots_adjust(hspace=0.75, bottom=0.25, top=0.9)
g.fig.suptitle("Frequency of Delay Causes Across Arrival Delay Intervals", fontsize=14, y=0.98)

plt.show()

The primary driver of minor delays (15 to 30 minutes) is the National Airspace System.

When the delay increases, Late aircraft becomes the dominant cause.

In all the delay groups, Late Aircraft, NAS and Carrier are the main delay drivers.

Now that we have looked at the cause of the delays and we have found a linear relationship between departure delays and arrival delays, let's look at the flight performance. How much do they recover in air?

Looking at the graphs we can notice:

  • Scheduled duration seem well planned as the CRSElapsedTime and ActualElapsedTime graph follow the y=x diagonal
  • Flights taking off on time tend to land on time while flights delayed at departure tend to be delayed at arrival
  • A long AirTime do not enable to catch up on departure delays since the delayed departure tends to be on the higher ArrDelay side.
  • The diagonal histograms show that most flights are short and on time

Talk about some of the relationships you observed in this part of the investigation. Were there features that strengthened each other in terms of looking at your feature(s) of interest?¶

  • Carrier delays seems to highly contribute to arrival delays but a lot of flights have several causes for arrival delays.
  • The long distance to travel does not seem to cause more or less delays. Long distance flights do not catchup either on late departure.
  • The scheduled airtime are generally well estimated compared to the actual airtime

Were there any interesting or surprising interactions between features?¶

  • The long distance does not seem to enable recovery on departure delay.
  • A lot of the arrival delays are caused by a single cause

Conclusions¶

In this analysis we looked at the arrival delays and their causes.

  • We discovered that the departure and arrival delays follow a heavy right tailed empirical distribution where most of the flights are on time but the disrupted flights can be severely delayed.
  • There is a linear relationship almost on the y=x diagonal between the departure delays and the arrival delays, meaning that a delayed departure almost guarantee a delayed arrival.
  • The on time performance varies from one airline to the other, with 2 airlines (Hawaiian Airlines - HA - and Aloha Air Cargo - KH -) outperforming others.
  • Flight distance does not enable recovery on delayed flights
  • Late aircraft is the primary delay cause, followed by carrier delays.
